## What this page is

A guided look at a real methylation project in a genome browser. We will walk through it together in class. You can also click through it on your own; nothing here needs to be installed or turned in.

The example is the Roberts Lab [Lake Trout EpiGenomics Project](https://robertslab.github.io/project-lake-trout/).

## The project in one paragraph

Lake trout (*Salvelinus namaycush*) in the Great Lakes come in two ecotypes that share the same water but live differently. **Lean** fish live in shallow water and carry little fat. **Siscowet** fish live deep and store a lot of lipid. The project sequenced four fish of each ecotype with PacBio HiFi long reads. Those reads carry the DNA sequence and, at the same time, the methylation state of each CpG (5mC). The question is which parts of the genome differ between the ecotypes, in sequence and in methylation.

## How methylation data become a browser track

1. **Reads to genome.** Long reads are aligned to a reference genome (here NCBI SaNama_1.0, plus lean and siscowet assemblies built for the project).
2. **Per-CpG methylation.** For each CpG, the fraction of reads that are methylated is computed for each fish. This is a table of chromosome, position, and percent methylation.
3. **Differential methylation.** CpGs (DMCs) or short regions (DMRs) that differ between ecotypes are called with a statistical test.
4. **Into the browser.** Each of those tables becomes a track: per-sample CpG methylation, DMR intervals, gene annotation, and other evidence such as presence/absence variation (PAV).

A track is just a file with coordinates. If the coordinates and genome version match, the browser can stack it under the others.

## Open the browsers

| Browser | What it is good for | Link |
|---|---|---|
| IGV.js | Fast look at genes, PAV, per-sample CpG methylation, and DMRs on the reference | [Launch IGV](https://robertslab.github.io/project-lake-trout/genome-browser/index.html) |
| JBrowse 2 | The same tracks on all three assemblies, plus a lean ↔ siscowet synteny view | [Launch JBrowse 2](https://robertslab.github.io/project-lake-trout/jbrowse/index.html) |

## What we will look at in class

**1. Orient yourself.** Before looking at any data, name the genome build and the chromosome or scaffold you are on. A coordinate means nothing without them.

**2. Read the tracks top to bottom.** Genes and exons, then the eight per-fish CpG methylation tracks (four lean, four siscowet), then the DMR and PAV tracks. Ask what each row is and where it came from.

**3. Find a DMR and zoom in.** Do all four fish of one ecotype look alike? Is the difference a few CpGs or a broad region? Is it in a gene, a promoter, or between genes?

**4. Check the context.** Is there a PAV or structural difference at the same spot? If part of the sequence is missing in one ecotype, a "methylation difference" there may really be a sequence difference.

**5. Compare to the summary page.** The project page lists candidate genes such as *gpia* and *ttll9*, and it explains which earlier findings did *not* hold up once each ecotype's own genome was assembled. Seeing a region in the browser is how you judge whether a table row is believable.

## Lessons the example teaches

- **Coordinates need a genome version.** The same DMR has different coordinates on the reference and on each ecotype assembly.
- **The reference can bias results.** The reference genome came from a lean fish, so siscowet reads that align poorly can look like deletions or methylation differences that are not real.
- **Repeats and multi-copy regions mislead.** About half of the original reference DMRs fell in multi-copy sequence.
- **Genetics and methylation are tangled.** Many DMRs sit near sequence differences, and methylation often follows the haplotype.
- **Small n, no validation.** Four fish per ecotype is enough to generate hypotheses, not to prove function. The project page says so directly, and that kind of statement belongs in your own reports too.

## Want to try it on your own project? (optional)

If you have a BAM, BED, VCF, or coverage file and a matching genome, you can load them into [IGV desktop](https://igv.org/doc/desktop/) or the [IGV web app](https://igv.org/app/) and look at one region that matters to you. This is a good habit before trusting any result, but it is not required this week.
